headline: 18.1 million people in Bangladesh at risk of severe food insecurity, WFP warns
summary: A new WFP report reveals a 2.8 million increase in people facing acute food insecurity since early this year, driven by high inflation, reduced purchasing power, and agricultural losses.
details: Around 18.1 million people in Bangladesh are projected to face severe food insecurity between September and December this year, according to a report by the World Food Programme (WFP). This marks an increase of 2.8 million people compared to the beginning of the year.

The WFP report, published on September 22, highlights several contributing factors including persistent high inflation, diminished purchasing power, agricultural damage from floods, widespread child malnutrition, and uncertainty regarding food assistance for Rohingya refugees.

The report coincides with World Food Day on October 16, celebrated under the theme 'Today's innovation, tomorrow's nutrition.' Bangladesh has been grappling with prolonged high inflation, low economic growth, and reduced employment opportunities.

The WFP report also notes that food insecurity and malnutrition are hindering child development. One in four children under five is stunted (low height-for-age), and 11% are wasted (low weight-for-height), with two out of five families experiencing significant micronutrient deficiencies.

In 2026, floods and waterlogging damaged approximately 80,000 hectares of agricultural land, affecting 230,000 farming families and 1.3 million people. This disruption has impacted food production and livelihoods across the country.

Global and regional risks also influence Bangladesh's food security. Nearly half of the country's remittances come from the Middle East, and there are concerns about potential disruptions to this vital income flow.

Food price inflation in Bangladesh surged after the Russia-Ukraine war began in early 2022, peaking at over 14% in July 2024 – the highest in over a decade. While it has now fallen below 10%, this indicates a slower rate of increase, not a reduction in prices.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecasted on October 13 that Bangladesh's GDP growth could slow to 3.2% in the current 2026-27 fiscal year, with average inflation potentially rising to 10.9%. This raises new concerns for economic recovery and purchasing power.

According to the Trading Corporation of Bangladesh (TCB), coarse rice and open flour currently cost at least BDT 50 per kilogram. Despite a good stock of 2.35 million tons of food grains, distribution under various programs has decreased.

Professor Salim Raihan of Dhaka University emphasized that the government's priority should be to identify and provide effective assistance to the most vulnerable populations. This includes expanding food aid, fair-price essential goods, and targeted cash support for low-income families and disaster-affected areas.
Professor Raihan also stressed the importance of regular market monitoring to prevent artificial crises, hoarding, and manipulation, ensuring transparency in the supply chain.

headline_marked: [[Cocktail bomb explodes]] near NCP office in Banglamotor, Dhaka; police disarm two others
headline: Cocktail bomb explodes near NCP office in Banglamotor, Dhaka; police disarm two others
summary: A cocktail bomb exploded near the National Citizens' Party (NCP) central office in Dhaka's Banglamotor area late Thursday night. Police later disarmed two unexploded devices found at the scene.
details: A cocktail bomb exploded on the road adjacent to the central office of the National Citizens' Party (NCP) in Dhaka's Banglamotor area. The incident occurred late Thursday night, around 12:30 AM.
Unidentified miscreants on a motorcycle threw three cocktail bombs in front of the NCP office. One of these devices detonated, while the other two remained unexploded.
Police officials promptly arrived at the scene following the incident. They successfully defused the two remaining unexploded cocktail bombs, ensuring public safety.
caption:
